This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

Cost leadership gets confused with saving money. Saving money is what happens in a bad quarter: budgets get cut, and six months later the costs are back and some good people are not.

Cost leadership is a property of how the company is built

It means being structurally cheaper than your competitors — profitable at a price where they break even. That is a very different thing from a decision to spend less, and the difference is where the advantage lives. A decision lives in a spreadsheet and can be reversed by the next person in the chair. A structure lives in processes, in the operating model, in how work moves through the company, and a competitor cannot copy it in a quarter because it took you longer than that to build. Which is why this course spends more time on process chains than on budget lines.

What this course covers

Forty-two lessons from the model down to a single cost line. The operating model first: what an efficiency-driven business is and which financial measures show it, turning strategy into financial goals, how models evolve from start-up to corporation, mission embedded into planned indicators, process chains and the black holes inside them, goal-setting people believe, the strategy pyramid, budgeting that produces decisions rather than documents, indicators across customers, people, processes and finance without killing motivation, Lean Six Sigma applied to financial processes, scaling without rebuilding, and what comes after efficiency. Then running the operation: the efficiency checklist, the strategy session and seven levels of strategy, culture as a delivery instrument with ten ways to embed it, the goal system and its launch, process building and automation, organisational structure with its five drivers and a diagnostic, project delivery templates, cash flow and monthly reporting, infrastructure including procurement and risk, and people management with the accountability table. Then describing processes: what a description consists of, which to describe first, methodology and a simple BPMN diagram, tools and templates, implementation and evaluation, five processes taken apart, and running the description project including defending it to management. Then improving them: waste, standardisation and maturity, five kinds of process map including the value stream, the improvement framework and its link to strategy, process architecture, the problem-solving toolkit from 5S and five whys to 8D and cause-and-effect diagrams, the advanced set including SIPOC, DRIVE and ICOR, and the culture that keeps improvement alive. Finally one cost line taken to the bottom: reading a large recurring bill, allocation and internal chargeback, rightsizing and commitments, unit economics per user and per transaction, and a ninety-day rollout.

Two blocks carry examples from a support function

The process description block uses one lesson of six to take apart five specific processes — hiring, settling in, training, review and exit — because they are simple enough to show end to end and everybody recognises them. The methodology in the other five lessons has no industry attached. The cost management block was recorded around technology spending, which is a particular category rather than a universal one: the allocation, chargeback and unit economics machinery transfers to any large recurring cost, the examples do not. Everything else — the operating model, the operations role and the optimisation toolkit — is about a company rather than a department.

Being right is not persuasive. It is a prerequisite, and it is the part you have already done, and it is why you are stuck.

Why good arguments lose

Because almost no resistance is logical. The person nodding along in the meeting has a reason to prefer the current arrangement that they are not going to say out loud. The proposal you sent was clear, correct and unanswered. The team agreed to the change and then simply carried on as before. In each case you were arguing with the rational half of someone and the decision was being made by the other half, which does not respond to evidence and was never addressed.

What this course covers

Forty-two lessons across six ways people actually get moved. Writing first: why a message goes unread, applying persuasion structures to text, copywriting and story, using emotion without manipulating, building a real exchange rather than a broadcast, arguing from a weak position, and reaching someone who has already ignored you twice. Then asking instead of telling: the GROW model, nine principles, the balance wheel and scales, listening well enough that the real objection appears, identifying and using the other person's language, what separates a powerful question from an open one, and delivering a message so it holds. Then the room: Dale's cone, preparation, delivery styles, group dynamics and resistance, group norms, metaphor and parable as working devices, how to open and how to close, and doing it through a screen. Then contested ground: making the case for something people are defensive about, designing a session that changes perception, role-play and facilitation as tactics, and checking whether anything moved. Then driving action: eight standard failures, Kotter's model, building genuine urgency, the rider-elephant-path frame, vision, quick wins and making it stick. Finally across borders: context, feedback, argument, power distance, decision-making, constructive conflict and time.

Three of the six blocks were recorded for a people-function audience. The failure almost never happens at the analysis stage. Eighteen of the thirty-eight lessons work with people data — turnover, engagement, hiring funnels, employee value. By the end of this masterclass, you’ll stop doing repetitive work manually and start using smart automation techniques that make your work faster, cleaner, and more professional. Enroll now and take a big step toward becoming a high-value, efficient Office professional.

Free AZ-900: Microsoft Azure Fundamentals Course  | AZ-900, Microsoft Azure Fundamentals AZ900, Azure AZ900, AZ-900


Prepare for the Microsoft AZ-900: Azure Fundamentals Certification Exam with a comprehensive course designed to help you understand Microsoft Azure cloud concepts and successfully pass the AZ-900 certification.


Whether you are new to cloud computing or an IT professional looking to validate your cloud knowledge, this course will help you learn the core Microsoft Azure services, cloud computing models, identity and security concepts, governance tools, and pricing structures used in Azure.


These practice tests will help you:

• Simulate the real AZ-900 certification exam experience

• Identify weak areas before taking the exam

• Strengthen your understanding of Azure cloud concepts

• Improve your exam readiness and confidence


The practice tests are ideal for learners who want hands-on exam preparation with realistic certification questions.


AZ-900 Exam Domains Covered

This course follows the official Microsoft AZ-900 skills outline, ensuring complete coverage of the certification exam topics. The AZ-900 exam measures your knowledge across three major domains.


Describe cloud concepts (25–30%)

Describe cloud computing

  • Define cloud computing

  • Describe the shared responsibility model

  • Define cloud models, including public, private, and hybrid

  • Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud model

  • Describe the consumption-based model

  • Compare cloud pricing models

  • Describe serverless

Describe the benefits of using cloud services

  • Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud

  • Describe the benefits of reliability and predictability in the cloud

  • Describe the benefits of security and governance in the cloud

  • Describe the benefits of manageability in the cloud

Describe cloud service types

  • Describe infrastructure as a service (IaaS)

  • Describe platform as a service (PaaS)

  • Describe software as a service (SaaS)

  • Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud service type (IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS)
targetAudiences: Beginners preparing for the Microsoft Azure AZ-900 certification exam
Students and freshers starting a career in cloud computing
IT professionals looking to learn Microsoft Azure fundamentals
Non-technical professionals interested in understanding cloud computing concepts
Anyone who wants to build a strong foundation in Microsoft Azure from scratch
